## Dermatoscopy (Table 3)

<mark>Dermatoscopy enhances the clinical diagnosis of AK, with reported sensitivity and specificity of **98.7%** and **95.0%**, respectively.</mark> <mark>Dermoscopic findings vary by clinical grade:</mark>

- <mark>**Grade 1 AK**: Red network pattern</mark>  
- <mark>**Grade 2 AK**: "Strawberry pattern" — background erythema with white-colored follicular openings, sometimes filled with keratin plugs</mark>  
- <mark>**Grade 3 AK**: Structureless white to yellow areas</mark>  

<mark>Dermatoscopy aids in differentiating:</mark>
- <mark>**Solitary AK grade III** (structureless yellow-white areas, focal strawberry pattern) from **Bowen’s disease** (coiled vessels)</mark>  
- <mark>**Pigmented AK** from **lentigo maligna**, based on:</mark>
  <mark>- Enlarged white follicular openings</mark>  
  <mark>- Double lines between hair follicles</mark>  
  <mark>- Background erythema</mark>  
  <mark>- Scaly surface</mark>  

<mark>In non-facial locations, follicular findings are less prominent; dermatoscopy typically shows erythema and superficial scales.</mark>

<mark>Dermatoscopy also helps detect early signs of **iSCC**, such as:</mark>
- <mark>Coiled or glomerular vessels</mark>  
- <mark>Polymorphous vessels</mark>  
- <mark>White circles</mark>  
<mark>These features are rarely seen in typical AK.</mark>

---

## Confocal Microscopy and Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) (Table 4)

**Reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM)** and **optical coherence tomography (OCT)**, when used alongside clinical examination and dermatoscopy, can assist in the differential diagnosis of:
- **AK vs. SCC**

## Fifth Disease (Erythema Infectiosum)

<mark>Fifth disease, the most common clinical manifestation of parvovirus B19 infection, typically begins with nonspecific symptoms such as headache, coryza, and low-grade fever, occurring approximately 2 days before the onset of the rash.</mark> <mark>During the rash phase, patients may experience additional symptoms including headache, pharyngitis, fever, malaise, myalgias, coryza, diarrhea, nausea, cough, and conjunctivitis.</mark>

<mark>Approximately 10% of children with erythema infectiosum develop arthralgias or arthritis.</mark> <mark>Large joints are more commonly affected than small joints.</mark> <mark>In rare cases, children may present with chronic joint complaints that resemble juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.</mark>

### Clinical Presentation of the Rash

<mark>The characteristic rash begins with bright red, confluent, erythematous, and edematous plaques on the malar eminences, producing the classic "slapped cheek" appearance.</mark> <mark>As the facial rash fades over 1 to 4 days, a secondary rash appears on the trunk, neck, and extensor surfaces of the extremities.</mark> <mark>This rash consists of pink to erythematous macules or papules with central clearing, giving it a lacy or reticulated appearance.</mark>

<mark>The rash may present in various morphologies, including morbilliform, confluent, circinate, or annular patterns, and involvement of the palms and soles has been reported.</mark> <mark>The eruption typically lasts 5 to 9 days but may recur intermittently for weeks or even months, triggered by factors such as sunlight, exercise, temperature changes, bathing, or emotional stress.</mark> <mark>Pruritus can be a prominent feature in some pediatric cases.</mark>

### <mark>Other Manifestations</mark>

<mark>Parvovirus B19 has been occasionally associated with vascular purpura, including Henoch-Schönlein purpura.</mark> <mark>An enanthem may also occur, characterized by erythema of the tongue and pharynx, along with red macules on the buccal mucosa and palate.</mark>

## <mark>Parvovirus B19 in Adults</mark>

<mark>In adults, acute arthropathy is the predominant manifestation of parvovirus B19 infection.</mark> <mark>It occurs more frequently in women and primarily affects the small joints of the hands and knees, although other joints such as those in the spine and costochondral joints may also be involved.</mark> <mark>The arthritis is typically symmetric, of sudden onset, and self-limited, though it can persist or recur for months.</mark> <mark>It may clinically mimic Lyme arthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.</mark>

<mark>Constitutional symptoms tend to be more severe in adults than in children.</mark> <mark>The typical presentation includes fever, adenopathy, and mild arthritis, often without a rash.</mark> <mark>Women are more likely than men to develop joint symptoms and rash, whereas men frequently present with a flu-like illness alone.</mark> <mark>Some adults experience prolonged fatigue, malaise, and depression following infection.</mark>

<mark>Asymptomatic infections occur in both adults and children; in one outbreak, 26% of infected adults were asymptomatic.</mark> <mark>Parvovirus B19 can also cause paresthesias, such as numbness and tingling of the fingers, with or without other signs of fifth disease.</mark> <mark>Pruritus, sometimes severe, may occur with or without a rash.</mark> <mark>Notably, the presence of pruritus in a patient with acute-onset arthritis should prompt consideration of parvovirus B19 infection as a potential cause.</mark>

# <mark>Sensory Nerves</mark>

<mark>The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) provides the majority of the sensory innervation of the face.</mark> It exits the skull via three foramina located bilaterally in the mid-pupillary line: the supraorbital, infraorbital, and mental foramina.

<mark>The first branch, the ophthalmic nerve $(\mathrm{V}_1)$, has several branches that supply the superior portion of the face: the supraorbital, supratrochlear, infratrochlear, external nasal, and lacrimal nerves.</mark> <mark>The supraorbital (lateral) and supratrochlear (medial) nerves supply the forehead and anterior scalp and are branches of the frontal nerve—the largest branch of the ophthalmic nerve.</mark> <mark>These nerves exit through notches along the orbital rim: the supraorbital foramen or notch laterally, and the supratrochlear notch medially.</mark> <mark>The infratrochlear nerve (a branch of the nasociliary nerve) supplies the glabella, nasal root, and bridge.</mark> <mark>The external nasal branch (also known as the dorsal nasal nerve), a terminal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve from the nasociliary branch of $\mathrm{V}_1$, innervates the dorsal nose.</mark> <mark>This provides the anatomical basis for Hutchinson sign in herpes zoster involving the ophthalmic nerve—vesicles on the nasal tip suggest possible ocular involvement because the nasociliary branch sends sensory fibers to both the nasal tip and the cornea.</mark> <mark>The lacrimal branch of $\mathrm{V}_1$ supplies sensation to the upper eyelid.</mark>

The second branch of the trigeminal nerve is the maxillary nerve $(\mathrm{V}_2)$. It provides sensory innervation to the lateral nose, lower eyelid, superior cheek, and anterior temple. The maxillary nerve gives rise to two main cutaneous branches: the zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal nerves. The zygomaticofacial nerve exits through the zygomatic bone and supplies a small area around the lateral canthus. The zygomaticotemporal nerve exits through the anterior temporal fossa and innervates the skin of the anterior temporal region. The largest branch of $\mathrm{V}_2$ is the infraorbital nerve, which exits the skull via the infraorbital foramen of the maxilla and supplies sensation to the lower eyelid and superior cheek.

The third branch of the trigeminal nerve is the mandibular nerve $(\mathrm{V}_3)$. Its cutaneous branches provide sensory innervation to the lower lip, chin, mandibular and preauricular cheek, anterior ear, and central temporal scalp. The three major cutaneous branches are the auriculotemporal, buccal, and mental nerves. The auriculotemporal nerve innervates the temple, temporoparietal scalp, anterior ear, parts of the external ear canal, and the tympanic membrane. The buccal nerve runs deep to the parotid gland and supplies the skin over the buccinator muscle, buccal mucosa, and gingiva. The mental nerve exits through the mental foramen as a continuation of the inferior alveolar nerve and provides sensation to the lower lip and chin.

# Muscles

The scalp contains two muscles: the frontalis anteriorly and the occipitalis posteriorly. These are connected by a tough, fibrous layer called the galea aponeurotica, which spans the cranial vault. The frontalis muscle covers the forehead and elevates the eyebrows. Medial and downward movement of the eyebrows occurs with contraction of the corrugator supercilii muscles. The procerus muscle, located between the corrugator supercilii muscles, pulls the skin of the forehead downward, contributing to horizontal creases at the root of the nose. The orbicularis oculi muscle surrounds the eye and consists of two parts: the orbital portion (involved in forceful eyelid closure) and the palpebral portion (responsible for gentle blinking).

## <mark>Herpes Zoster: Clinical Features and Complications</mark>

### <mark>Dermatomal Involvement and Rash Evolution</mark>
- **Early stage**: Characterized by erythema within a thoracic dermatome, followed by grouped vesicle formation.
- **Later stage**: Crusted lesions appear on the back (site of initial eruption), with newer, confluent hemorrhagic vesicles and bullae on the lateral chest wall. Vesicles extending beyond the primary dermatome suggest hematogenous dissemination, which is not uncommon.

- Crusting typically persists for 2–3 weeks.
- New lesions usually appear for 1–4 days, occasionally up to 7 days in immunocompetent individuals.
- Rash severity and duration are greatest in older adults and mildest in children.

### <mark>Ophthalmic Zoster</mark>
- <mark>Involves the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve in 10%–15% of herpes zoster cases.</mark>
- <mark>Rash distribution extends from the eye to the skull vertex, stopping sharply at the midline of the forehead.</mark>
- <mark>Isolated involvement of the **supraorbital** and **supratrochlear** nerves usually spares the eye.</mark>
- <mark>**Nasociliary nerve** involvement (which innervates the eye and nasal tip) increases risk of ocular complications.</mark>
- <mark>**Hutchinson’s sign**: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose indicate potential ocular involvement, necessitating ophthalmologic evaluation.</mark>
- <mark>Ocular involvement occurs in 30%–40% of ophthalmic zoster cases.</mark>
- <mark>Common complications include impaired corneal sensation, **neurotrophic keratitis**, and chronic corneal ulceration.</mark>

### Cranial Nerve Involvement
- Herpes zoster affecting the **mandibular** and **maxillary** divisions of the trigeminal nerve or other cranial nerves may cause lesions in the mouth, pharynx, larynx, or ears.
- **Ramsay Hunt syndrome**: Results from facial (VII) and auditory (VIII) nerve involvement.
  - Presents with facial palsy, vesicles on the external ear or tympanic membrane.
  - May include tinnitus, vertigo, and sensorineural hearing loss.

### Pain in Herpes Zoster
- Pain is the most significant symptom, particularly in elderly patients.
- Acute-phase pain (within 30 days of rash onset) ranges from mild to severe.
- Described as burning, aching, tingling, itching, or stabbing.
- Some patients report excruciating or unbearable pain.
- Associated with reduced physical function, emotional distress, and impaired social functioning.

### Herpes Zoster in Immunocompromised Hosts
- Immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk for severe complications beyond postherpetic neuralgia (PHN).
- Common complications:
  - Skin necrosis and scarring.
  - Cutaneous dissemination (25%–50% incidence).
  - Visceral dissemination (in ~10% of disseminated cases), often involving lungs, liver, and brain; may be fatal.
- **HIV-infected patients**:
  - Prone to multiple recurrences of herpes zoster as immune function declines.
  - Recurrences may occur in the same, different, or multiple contiguous/non-contiguous dermatomes.
  - In AIDS, zoster can be severe, with widespread cutaneous and visceral dissemination.

## Myalgias and Musculoskeletal Concerns
Myalgias are the most common musculoskeletal complaint, occurring in 15 percent of patients. In severe cases, creatine phosphokinase levels should be evaluated to assess for possible rhabdomyolysis.

## <mark>Isotretinoin Therapy: Teratogenicity and Contraception</mark>
<mark>The greatest concern during isotretinoin therapy is the risk of administration during pregnancy, which can lead to severe teratogenic effects in the fetus.</mark> <mark>The drug is not mutagenic; its adverse effects occur during organogenesis.</mark> <mark>Therefore, isotretinoin should be reserved for patients who have not responded to other treatments.</mark>

<mark>Women of childbearing age must be fully informed of the risks associated with pregnancy while on isotretinoin.</mark> <mark>Patients must use two highly effective forms of contraception—such as an oral contraceptive combined with condoms and spermicidal jelly—starting at least one month before beginning therapy.</mark> <mark>Female patients must be thoroughly counseled and demonstrate understanding of contraceptive methods prior to treatment initiation.</mark> <mark>Dual contraception must continue throughout isotretinoin therapy and for one month after discontinuation.</mark>

<mark>In the United States, the FDA requires a strict risk management program known as iPledge.</mark> <mark>This computer-based system ensures adherence to pregnancy prevention protocols before, during, and after isotretinoin treatment.</mark>

## <mark>Dosing and Treatment Duration</mark>
<mark>The recommended daily dosage of isotretinoin is 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day.</mark> <mark>A cumulative weight-based dosing target of 120 to 150 mg/kg over the course of therapy is often used, particularly in patients with variable dosing or interrupted treatment, as achieving this total dose improves the likelihood of long-term remission.</mark>

<mark>Patients with severe truncal acne—especially those with back and chest lesions, which respond less robustly than facial lesions—may require higher doses, up to 2 mg/kg/day.</mark> 

<mark>In patients with severe acne, particularly those with granulomatous lesions, disease flares are common at treatment initiation.</mark> <mark>To mitigate this, initial dosing should be low—often below 0.5 mg/kg/day.</mark> <mark>Pre-treatment with prednisone (40 to 60 mg/day) for 1 to 2 weeks may be necessary and sometimes continued for the first two weeks of isotretinoin therapy.</mark>

<mark>A typical course lasts 20 weeks, but duration is flexible.</mark> <mark>Therapy may be extended in patients who do not achieve adequate response.</mark> <mark>Additional improvement may occur for 1 to 2 months after stopping treatment, so complete clearance is not required before discontinuation.</mark>

## <mark>Laboratory Monitoring</mark>
<mark>Baseline laboratory tests should include a complete blood count and liver function tests.</mark> <mark>However, the most critical monitoring involves serum triglyceride levels.</mark>

- <mark>Baseline triglycerides should be measured before starting therapy.</mark>
- <mark>Repeat testing is recommended at 3 to 4 weeks and again at 6 to 8 weeks.</mark>
- <mark>If levels are normal at 6 to 8 weeks and no risk factors are present, further testing may not be needed.</mark>
- <mark>If triglycerides exceed 500 mg/dL, monitoring should be frequent.</mark>
- <mark>Levels above 700–800 mg/dL warrant interruption of therapy or initiation of lipid-lowering treatment.</mark>
- <mark>Complications such as eruptive xanthomas or pancreatitis can occur at very high triglyceride levels.</mark>

## <mark>Diet and Acne</mark>
Several studies have suggested a potential role for diet in acne development. However, the overall evidence remains inconclusive. The impact of chocolate, sweets, milk, and fatty foods on acne requires further investigation. There is no strong evidence supporting routine elimination of these foods. Nevertheless, some patients report disease flares after consuming specific foods—particularly chocolate. Given these individual perceptions, it is reasonable to advise patients to avoid dietary items they believe trigger their acne.

## Acne Surgery
Acne surgery, involving the removal of comedones and superficial pustules, can accelerate the resolution of individual acne lesions. It was historically a mainstay of acne treatment.

# Comparison of guidelines and consensus articles on the management of patients with acne with oral isotretinoin

## Abstract

Guidelines and consensus statements on the management of acne aim to provide evidence-based, expert-driven recommendations. This review compares current guidelines and consensus articles to compile recommendations on the use of oral isotretinoin in acne treatment. Ten common and clinically relevant questions are addressed, including indications for isotretinoin, recommended daily and cumulative doses, treatment duration, and laboratory monitoring. Special considerations such as timing of dermatologic procedures and potential associations with depression or inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are also evaluated. A major limitation across guidelines is the use of differing acne classification systems. The recommended daily dose ranges from 0.3 to 0.5 mg/kg in European guidelines to up to 1 mg/kg in U.S. guidelines. Only European guidelines specify a minimum treatment duration of 6 months. All guidelines emphasize strict pregnancy prevention due to teratogenicity. Monitoring for symptoms of depression is recommended in European, French, and U.S. guidelines. Key clinical issues that remain inconsistently addressed include age indications, target cumulative dose, timing of procedures, isotretinoin-IBD association, acne flare prevention, and laboratory monitoring protocols. These topics require clearer inclusion in future guidelines, as they frequently arise in clinical practice.

## Introduction

Oral isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid), a natural metabolite of vitamin A, was approved for the treatment of acne vulgaris in 1982 by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and in 1983 by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). Isotretinoin undergoes rapid intracellular conversion to all-trans retinoic acid and exhibits strong biological activity with low binding affinity for retinoid receptors. It effectively inhibits sebocyte proliferation, differentiation, and lipid synthesis both in vivo and in vitro, reduces *Cutibacterium acnes* (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*) colonization, and decreases inflammation and hyperkeratinization within the pilosebaceous unit.

The efficacy and safety of oral isotretinoin were evaluated in a systematic review by Vallerand et al., which included 11 randomized controlled trials published up to 2016. All studies demonstrated a clinically significant reduction in acne lesions with isotretinoin compared to control groups (placebo, systemic antibiotics, or other comparators). Adverse events occurred approximately twice as often with isotretinoin versus controls. Most were cutaneous and related to xerosis. Serious adverse events leading to discontinuation included Stevens-Johnson syndrome, severe cheilitis, photophobia, elevated liver enzymes, anorexia, headache, and depression.

This review compares current international and national guidelines and consensus statements on the use of oral isotretinoin for acne. Guidelines are intended to optimize patient care through evidence-based, critically appraised recommendations on treatment benefits and risks. Key areas of focus include indications for use, dosing strategies (daily and cumulative), treatment duration, laboratory monitoring, and special considerations such as procedural timing and potential psychiatric or gastrointestinal risks.

## Methods

Eligible publications included updated international and national guidelines and consensus articles containing recommendations on oral isotretinoin for acne. EMA recommendations were included as they inform drug prescribing frameworks in Europe. Guidelines published before 2012 or without a stated validity date were excluded. Only publications in English or French were considered.

Search terms included: *isotretinoin*, *systemic treatment*, *acne*, *guidelines*, *consensus*. Reference lists of included articles were manually screened for additional relevant guidelines or consensus documents. The final literature search was conducted on 20 May 2019.

# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

## <mark>Skin and Mucous Membrane Involvement</mark>

<mark>The characteristic skin lesion of bullous pemphigoid is a large, tense blister that arises on normal-appearing skin or on an erythematous base.</mark> These lesions most commonly occur on the lower abdomen, inner or anterior thighs, and flexor surfaces of the forearms, although they can appear anywhere on the body. <mark>The bullae are typically filled with clear fluid but may be hemorrhagic.</mark> <mark>After rupture, the erosions usually reepithelialize well and do not expand peripherally, unlike in pemphigus vulgaris.</mark> <mark>New vesicles may, however, develop at the edges of resolving lesions.</mark> <mark>Bullous pemphigoid lesions do not scar, and pruritus is commonly present, though not universally.</mark>

<mark>In some cases, the erythematous component predominates, and patients may initially present with urticarial plaques, particularly early in the disease course.</mark> <mark>The erythema can have a serpiginous pattern with peripheral blistering and may be extensive.</mark> Healing typically begins in the center of the lesions and may be accompanied by hyperpigmentation.

Mucous membrane involvement occurs in approximately 10% to 35% of patients and is almost always confined to the oral mucosa, particularly the buccal mucosa. Lesions may appear as intact blisters or, more commonly, as erosions. These do not scar and are usually not widespread. Notably, the vermilion border of the lips is rarely affected, distinguishing it from erythema multiforme.

## Unusual Clinical Presentations

<mark>Bullous pemphigoid can present in atypical forms, all confirmed by characteristic immunofluorescence findings.</mark> In some cases, the disease is localized, most frequently to the lower legs. Patients with localized disease have antibodies against the same pemphigoid antigens (BP180 and BP230) as those with generalized disease and may either remain localized for years or progress to generalized involvement.

A distinct variant occurs in young girls, characterized by blisters and erosions limited to the vulvar and perivulvar regions. As in other localized and childhood forms, autoantibodies target the classic pemphigoid antigens.

<mark>Early in the disease, some patients may exhibit only urticarial or eczematous lesions without frank bullae.</mark> Other rare presentations include erythroderma, prurigo nodularis-like lesions, vegetating lesions, and dyshidrotic dermatitis-like eruptions. <mark>Despite the atypical morphology, the immunopathological findings—such as linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone and reactivity with BPAG2 (BP180)—remain consistent with bullous pemphigoid.</mark>

## <mark>Diagnosis in DIF-Negative Patients</mark>

<mark>In the few patients with persistent negative direct immunofluorescence (DIF) studies, the diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid (BP) can be accepted if one or more of the following criteria are met:</mark>

- <mark>**Suggestive clinical picture**, such as tense blisters;</mark>
- <mark>**Consistent histopathological findings**, specifically subepidermal cleavage;</mark>
- <mark>**Presence of circulating IgG autoantibodies** binding to the epidermal side of split-skin substrate (SSS) on indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) microscopy;</mark>
- <mark>**Serum reactivity against BP180 and/or BP230** detected by ELISA or IIF.</mark>

## <mark>Additional Diagnostic Tests</mark>

<mark>Additional tests may be performed based on clinical context and availability.</mark> <mark>Refer to Table 1 for further details [25,34–38].</mark>

# Therapeutic Management (see Tables 2 and 3)

## Workup and Pretreatment Screening

A comprehensive pretreatment evaluation is recommended and outlined in Table 2. These recommendations are primarily based on expert opinion and should be adapted according to updated guidelines and local healthcare practices.

### Table 2: Suggested Workup and Pretreatment Screening in Newly Diagnosed Bullous Pemphigoid

- Chest X-ray  
- Complete blood count (CBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP)  
- Creatinine, blood electrolytes, and fasting glucose  
- Liver function tests: transaminases, gamma-glutamyl transferase (gamma-GT), alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin  
- Albumin  
- Serology for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV (if immunosuppressive therapy is planned)  
- Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age (rare in BP) prior to starting treatment  
- Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) testing (optional, if azathioprine is considered)  
- Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) testing (if dapsone is considered)  
- Exclude serum IgA deficiency (if intravenous immunoglobulin therapy is planned)  
- Consider detailed neurological examination and brief cognitive assessment (e.g., Mini-Mental State Examination)  
- Evaluate for underlying malignancy based on age, history, and physical findings  
- Screen for infections, particularly *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, when immunosuppression is indicated  
- Consider osteodensitometry (DEXA scan) if long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy is anticipated  
- Consider ocular examination (intraocular pressure and cataract screening) if long-term corticosteroid use is expected  
- Local bacteriological sampling if skin infection is clinically suspected  
- Consider echocardiography before initiating systemic corticosteroids, dapsone, or intravenous immunoglobulins  
- SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination: follow current national and international guidelines and public health recommendations

---

## Objectives of Management

Bullous pemphigoid is a chronic condition that typically lasts several months to years, particularly in patients experiencing multiple relapses [1,2,4,5].

### Primary Goals of Therapy:

- Control skin lesions and pruritus, and prevent or reduce the risk of recurrence;  
- Improve patient quality of life;  
- Minimize treatment-related adverse effects, especially in elderly patients.

Given that BP predominantly affects older adults, comorbidities such as neurological, cardiovascular, metabolic, thromboembolic, neoplastic, respiratory, ocular, and osteoporotic conditions often complicate management [1,2,19,39,40]. Therefore, treatment must be individualized, balancing efficacy with safety.

# Updated S2 K Guidelines for the Management of Bullous Pemphigoid Initiated by the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV)

## Abstract

<mark>**Background**</mark>  
<mark>Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease affecting the skin and mucous membranes.</mark> <mark>It primarily occurs in the elderly, presenting with pruritus and localized or generalized bullous lesions.</mark> <mark>A subset of patients may present with non-bullous manifestations such as excoriations, prurigo-like lesions, eczematous changes, or urticarial erythema.</mark> <mark>BP is significantly associated with neurological disorders, carries high morbidity, and markedly impairs quality of life.</mark>

**Objectives and Methodology**  
The Autoimmune Blistering Diseases Task Force of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology updated the management guidelines for BP based on emerging clinical evidence, diagnostic tools, and therapeutic interventions. <mark>Recommendations are either evidence-based or derived from expert consensus, with documentation of agreement among task force members.</mark>

**Results**  
Treatment selection depends on disease severity and patient comorbidities.  
- **High-potency topical corticosteroids** are recommended as first-line therapy whenever feasible.  
- **Oral prednisone at 0.5 mg/kg/day** is an alternative, particularly for more extensive disease.  
- In cases of corticosteroid contraindications or treatment resistance, **immunosuppressive agents** such as methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or mycophenolic acid may be used.  
- **Doxycycline and dapsone** have uncertain efficacy; however, they may be considered, especially in patients who cannot tolerate oral corticosteroids.  
- For refractory disease, **B-cell-depleting therapy (e.g., rituximab)** and **intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG)** are potential options.  
- Emerging biologics such as **omalizumab** and **dupilumab** have shown promising results in early studies.  

The final guideline version was endorsed by several patient organizations, emphasizing patient-centered care.

**Conclusions**  
These updated guidelines provide evidence- and expert opinion–based recommendations for the management of bullous pemphigoid, designed to support clinical decision-making.

## <mark>Introduction</mark>

<mark>Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most prevalent autoimmune subepidermal blistering dermatosis.</mark> <mark>It is characterized by tissue-bound and circulating autoantibodies targeting two components of hemidesmosomes: **BP180 (BPAG2 or type XVII collagen)** and **BP230 (BPAG1e, epithelial isoform)**.</mark> <mark>These proteins are critical for dermal-epidermal adhesion, and their autoimmune disruption leads to subepidermal blister formation.</mark>

<mark>BP predominantly affects individuals over 70 years of age, with a mean diagnosis age of approximately 80 years in Europe.</mark> <mark>The disease is marked by severe pruritus and cutaneous blistering, significantly impairing quality of life.</mark> <mark>It is associated with considerable morbidity and a two- to threefold increased mortality compared to age- and sex-matched controls.</mark>

<mark>The annual incidence ranges from 6 to 43 per million, with rising trends observed over the past two decades.</mark> <mark>This increase may be attributed to greater recognition of non-bullous presentations, a growing prevalence of neurological conditions (such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease) linked to BP, and increased use of medications implicated in BP induction—particularly **gliptins** and **immune checkpoint inhibitors**.</mark> <mark>These drug associations underscore the need for systematic evaluation of medication history and consideration of drug discontinuation in affected patients.</mark>

Updates to the management consensus were prompted by new randomized and open-label clinical trials evaluating immunomodulatory agents and biologics, advances in diagnostic methodologies, and a heightened focus on patient-reported outcomes such as quality of life. Shared decision-making between clinicians and patients is now recognized as a key component of treatment planning and should be integrated into routine practice.

# <mark>Laboratory investigations for the diagnosis of BP</mark>

<mark>Confirm the diagnosis of BP.</mark> <mark>The diagnosis is based on a combination of criteria encompassing clinical features, compatible light microscopy findings, and positive direct immunofluorescence microscopy (DIF) findings.</mark> <mark>The following steps are recommended for the diagnosis and classification of BP:</mark>

- Detection of circulating IgG anti-basement membrane zone (BMZ) autoantibodies by indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) microscopy using NaCl-separated normal human skin;  
- Detection of anti-BP180 NC16A IgG autoantibodies and/or anti-BP230 IgG autoantibodies by ELISA;  
- For detection of circulating IgG anti-BMZ autoantibodies, novel 'multivariant' IIF-based assays using multiple antigenic substrates are also recommended. In these BIOCHIP mosaic assays, various antigenic substrates are combined.

In rare cases of BP where circulating anti-BMZ antibodies are not detectable by IIF or commercially available ELISA, additional tests should be used to increase diagnostic sensitivity and to exclude other autoimmune diseases affecting the dermoepidermal junction, particularly anti-p200 pemphigoid or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA).

## <mark>Histopathology</mark>

<mark>Specimens for light microscopy should be taken from early bullae arising on erythematous skin and placed in formalin solution.</mark> <mark>Typical findings include subepidermal bullae containing eosinophils and/or neutrophils, associated with a dermal infiltrate of eosinophils and/or neutrophils, or a margination of eosinophils along the dermal-epidermal junction.</mark> <mark>However, in non-bullous forms or in the absence of blistering, histopathological findings may be nonspecific, such as eosinophilic spongiosis.</mark>

## <mark>Direct immunofluorescence microscopy</mark>

<mark>Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) studies are the most critical diagnostic test—positivity is essential for confirming BP.</mark> <mark>It is recommended to obtain the biopsy specimen for DIF from perilesional skin, defined as erythematous nonbullous skin or normal-appearing skin within 1–2 cm of a lesion.</mark>

<mark>For transportation, skin biopsy specimens should be placed in either 0.9% NaCl solution, a cryotube with liquid nitrogen, or Michel's fixative.</mark> <mark>Alternatively, for storage and transport, 0.9% NaCl (with processing required within 24–72 hours), liquid nitrogen in a cryotube, or Michel's medium may be used.</mark>

- <mark>DIF typically shows linear deposits of IgG and/or C3 along the dermo-epidermal junction; occasionally, IgA and IgE may also be present in a similar pattern;</mark>  
- <mark>Analysis of the n-serration pattern in DIF can be helpful and specific when combined with IIF to differentiate BP from EBA: an n-serrated pattern is suggestive of BP, whereas a u-serrated pattern is typically seen in EBA.</mark>
